summary.text: Hotspots are volcanic places thought to be fed by mantle rock hotter than the mantle around it, such as Hawaii, Iceland and Yellowstone.
A hotspot's position does not depend on plate boundaries, so a plate moving over it can build a chain of volcanoes, like the Hawaiian islands.
One idea says hotspots are fed by plumes rising from the core–mantle boundary; a rival idea says melt rises where the crust above is weak or thin.

facts.label: How many exist
facts.value: Most geologists think a few dozen are plume-fed

facts.label: Usual lava
facts.value: Basalt, as at Hawaii and Tahiti

facts.label: Best-imaged plume
facts.value: Yellowstone, traced from deep mantle to surface

items.prompt: Along the Hawaiian chain, islands get older and more worn down the farther northwest you go. What does that tell you?

options.label: The hot source itself is crawling northwest
The plate carried older islands off the hot source
Northwest islands simply erode faster in storms
The islands formed at random times and places

items.explain: With the feeder roughly fixed and the plate drifting overhead, a time-progressive chain forms, with the oldest islands farthest away.

items.prompt: Hawaii's volcanoes tend to be far less explosive than volcanoes above subduction zones. Why?

options.label: They are younger and have less pressure built up
Seawater around them cools the magma quickly
Their basalt magma lacks water from a sinking plate
They are much smaller than subduction volcanoes

items.explain: Most hotspot volcanoes are basaltic, while subduction volcanoes have water trapped under the overriding plate, which makes them more explosive.

items.prompt: A hotspot under a continent, like Yellowstone, can produce far more violent eruptions than one under the ocean. Why?

options.label: Continental plates move faster over hotspots
The magma there comes from a deeper source
Ice sheets on continents trap the volcanic gas
Rising basalt melts crust into explosive rhyolite

items.explain: Basaltic magma rising through continental crust melts it to form rhyolite, which can erupt violently, as at the Yellowstone Caldera.

items.prompt: What makes rock melt to feed the volcanoes of the Aleutian Islands near Alaska?

options.label: Water released from a sinking plate changes the rock above
A plume rising from the core–mantle boundary
Friction as two plates slide past each other sideways
Heat left over from a large meteorite impact

items.explain: These are island arc volcanoes: a subducting plate releases water into the plate above, changing its composition so some rock melts.

items.prompt: A geologist doubts that deep mantle plumes exist. How would she most likely explain a hotspot volcano?

options.label: Meteorites keep striking that same spot
Ocean water seeps down and boils the rock
Weak or thin crust lets shallow melt rise passively
The core has a bulge right beneath that spot

items.explain: The alternative plate theory says the mantle below is not unusually hot; the crust above is weak or thin, letting melt rise from shallow depths.

items.prompt: Geologists hoped hotspot volcano chains would act as fixed markers for tracking plate motion. What spoiled this?

options.label: Hotspots seem to shift relative to one another
Volcanic rocks cannot be dated at all
The plates turned out not to move
Every chain is far too long to map

items.explain: The effort is hampered by the lack of very long chains, chains that are not time-progressive, and hotspots that do not stay fixed relative to each other.
